=== near.py
near.py: the curator's messages in a window before a UTC time, each with the coordinating
session's message that it answered, found along the transcript's reply chain.

    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z            window 60 minutes before the time
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m        or 2h, 1d
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m --cut 2000
                                                        cut each printed text at 2000 characters
                                                        (his and the coordinator's), saying so;
                                                        by default every text is printed whole

For each message of his: its time, source (main, s1, queued: see show.py), session, length and
full text. Then the message he answered: the coordinator's turn that his message follows on the
reply chain (tlib.py says how the chain is read), every text of that turn whole, each with its
time and the file and line it was read from (the first copy, when a resumed transcript replays
it). Before it, one line for each turn the chain passed over as not addressed to him (replies to
Stop-hook feedback, to an agent's message or hand-back, to a task notification or check-in, to a
system reminder), and for each text written after he sent his message; a passed-over turn that
answers a notification and ends with an ask to him (a question mark, "The ask", "I recommend",
"your yes", ...) is marked, and the newest such turn printed whole, since he may have answered
it. When he quotes lines ("> ..."), the text on the chain that holds them is named, and printed
whole if it is not the answer. After it, the last lines of the three turns to him further back
on the chain, for a message that answers an older question. A queued message (sent while a turn
ran) starts at its delivery into the turn; texts written after he sent it are not taken. A
message on no chain the index holds (a queued one never delivered) falls back to the time: the
coordinator's last text before it, passing over replies to Stop-hook feedback.
=== later.py
later.py: his messages after an entry's creation that may bear on it, though no commit of the
entry followed them (his later word may have gone into a skill or another record instead).

    python3 -I later.py 148                   (or P-148)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --top 25          how many to print (default 15)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --at 36f7db77c --until 2026-10-21T20:54
                                              the entry's text at a commit, and no message after a time

The candidates are his messages in the coordinating sessions (tlib.COORDINATING) from the entry's
creation on (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md, its last text is read, and the list runs on
past the removal) (the first commit of its trail that made its text), less those that leads.py already
printed near the entry's own commits. Each is scored by the entry's distinctive terms:
  - its title's words, beyond common words (a stop list, and words in more than a tenth of his
    messages), lightly stemmed (possessive and plural off, cut to 7 letters); each weighs its
    rarity in his messages, log(messages / messages holding it);
  - its names in backticks, weight 3 each.
A term in his own words (lines that do not start with ">") counts whole; a term only in the
exchange around his message (the coordinator's message he answered, by the reply chain, its
reply to him, and the lines he quoted) counts half. A message also gains 8 when it falls in the
30 minutes before a commit that changed a file the entry names in backticks (`compiler.md`), other
than the entry's own commits, in lines that hold a title term (3 when the lines hold none): that
is where his word may have gone. Naming the entry's number (P-148, or as dictated, P148) adds 8 in
his words, 2 in the exchange. A message is a candidate when its weight is at least 5 (MIN) and it
holds a term in his own words or falls before such a commit. Printed: rank, weight, time, whether it
is after the entry's last change, the terms (in parentheses when only in the exchange), the commit
=== homes.py
homes.py: where a status that an entry of POSITIONS.md states may already live.

    python3 -I homes.py 151            (or P-151)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --top 8    candidates per sentence (default 5)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --at REV   the three files as commit REV holds them

Splits the entry (the working tree's POSITIONS.md; for an entry struck from it, its text as it
last stood, said so at the top) into sentences, and a sentence into its clauses
at the semicolons outside parentheses; a clause keeps the label that opens its sentence, as
"Built:" or "Still to build:". A clause states a status when it, its label or its sentence holds
one of the status words: built, to build, landed, pending, default, waits, standing go, listed for his
review, open, held, parked, owed, taken, stands at, returns after, not moved, and the like.

For each such clause it lists the candidates that may already hold the same point: the numbered
items of review-queue.md's lists (b) and (c), and the lines of PLAN.md (a numbered sub-line also
carries its parent's item number, and its own number as a fork when the parent counts forks).
A candidate is listed when it names the entry or shares a distinctive term with the clause:
  row N, item N (PLAN's), review-queue item N, fork N, way N, batch N, rung X, phase N, ask N,
  decision X, another entry's P-N, a name in backticks (a commit hash too), a dotted finding
  name such as judge-review.1 or A.skeptic.2
Each shared term weighs by its rarity among the candidates (log of the candidates over those
holding it); naming the entry adds 2; content words shared (four letters or more, beyond common
words) add a little, to order near-ties, and are printed apart. Candidates are ranked by that
weight, and each is printed with what it shares, for the scout to confirm or reject.

=== pointers.py
pointers.py: every line of the record that names an entry of POSITIONS.md by its number.

    python3 -I pointers.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I pointers.py 86 --at REV   the files as commit REV holds them

Searches, at the working tree: explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, POSITIONS.md, PLAN.md,
review-queue.md, HELD.md and BOOT.md; explorations/reviews/open-asks-*.md; and every file under
.claude/skills/. The history files (POSITIONS-history.md, FACTS-history.md) are not searched:
trail.py reads the first, and both only record. A line counts when it holds the number as a word:
P-86 matches, as in "P-86's" or "(P-86)", but P-860 and P-186 do not. A line that names a range
holding the number ("P-85 to P-88") is listed too, marked as a range.
Prints path:line and the line (cut at 400 characters around the number; --whole prints it whole),
grouped by file; the entry's own line in POSITIONS.md is marked.

=== comments.py
comments.py: his saved page comments that bear on an entry of POSITIONS.md.

    python3 -I comments.py 66            (or P-66)

He also comments on pages, and those comments are not in the transcripts. They are saved as
explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/evidence/curator-comments-*.md: a section per thread,
headed "## On <what it was anchored to>", with one bullet per comment, "- HH:MM: "words"".
A section counts when its heading, or a comment counts when its own words, either
  - name the entry's number, also as dictated: P-66, P66, PE66, P 66 (not P-660), or
  - quote its title: a quoted run ("..." or curly quotes) of at least three content words, at
    least 60 % of which are words of the entry's bold title (case, possessives and punctuation
    ignored).
A section that counts is printed whole, with its heading; a comment that counts in another
section is printed with that section's heading. Each with its file and line.

=== trail.py
trail.py: the trail of one entry of POSITIONS.md, from the repository's history.

    python3 -I trail.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --short    the commit list only, one line each
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --at REV   the record as commit REV holds it

Prints:
  1. the entry's text at HEAD (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md: STRUCK at the top, with the
     commit that removed it and the reason its history block gives, and the text as it last stood);
  2. its blocks in POSITIONS-history.md at HEAD, each with the commit that wrote it (the oldest
     commit whose history file holds the block's provenance line). A block's own "commit X" names
     the source it cites, not its writer;
  3. every commit that made or changed the entry's text, oldest first, read from each commit's own
     tree (side branches included): hash, UTC author time, subject, what it did, how the link to
     the text before was made (number, line, title: exact; similarity: score printed), how many
     other entries of POSITIONS.md the commit changed, and the reasons on record: the history
     blocks it wrote, the comments above verbatim copies of the text in the old history file, and
     the commit message.
  4. a cross-check: the old history lines that the numbering block names as earlier texts of this
     entry, and whether each is a text of this trail.

What a commit did:
  created          a text new in POSITIONS.md that no removed or earlier text explains
  changed          a text that replaced another of the same commit (link: number, line, title or similarity)
  moved to history the text left POSITIONS.md and stands verbatim in POSITIONS-history.md
=== quote.py
quote.py: does the curator's message at a UTC time hold a quote word for word?

    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21:32Z
    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21        a prefix: every message of his in that minute

The time is a prefix of his message's timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z is dropped).
For each message of his at that time it prints one verdict:
  EXACT        the quote is a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once both have every run of whitespace made one space, ends trimmed,
               and the curly apostrophe U+2019 made a straight one (nothing else is changed)
  NO MATCH     neither; it then prints the longest run of the quote's words that the
               message holds word for word (after the same normalising), for a reader to judge
With the match it prints the message's text around it.

=== hischeck.py
hischeck.py: check the block of his quotes that a scout's or reader's report ends with.

    python3 -I hischeck.py FILE...

Each FILE holds a block headed "## His quotes" (to the next "## " heading or the end), one line
per quote of his:
    HIS 2026-09-26T10:21:32.097Z | Run Fable judgement as well.
(a line may be wrapped in backticks or start with "- "). The time is a prefix of his message's
timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z dropped); each message of his at that time is tried,
and the quote is checked as quote.py does:
  EXACT        a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once whitespace is collapsed and U+2019 made a straight apostrophe
  NO MATCH     neither, in every message at that time (quote.py "QUOTE" TIME shows the nearest run)
  NO MESSAGE   no message of his at that time
Lines of the block that start with HIS but do not parse are counted as BAD FORM. Prints, per
file, the counts and every line that is not EXACT or NORMALISED, with its line number; exits 1
when any line fails or a file has no block.

content.content:
- As decided 2026-09-28: one Opus reviewer after every landing, reading only, before the next batch launches; the conformance review, the process measures and the routing check in one pass. It gains the merged-diff review's count-table check (each moved count row tied to a rung edit) and one paragraph, what the batch spent against what it changed.
- Reads: the landed tree, the reports, the gate's tables, and the transcripts where a question needs them.
- Commits: its review file only. Its measuring scripts are one shared tool under `coordinator/tools/`, not copied into each review's folder.

## 2. The four remaining questions

Each recommendation is the default from tonight and is listed for Pavol's review (section 6). Each is checked against the entries of POSITIONS named in the coordinator's brief: 2026-09-17 (test first, extended 2026-09-29), 2026-09-18, 2026-09-24, 2026-09-26, 2026-09-27, 2026-09-28 and the four of 2026-09-29.

### (a) The corpus-wide output comparison, run three times per rung

Default: removed as a standing rule. No rung runs the interpreter corpus to compare outputs. A value that matters is asserted in the rung's own test (`assert` in the interpreter corpus, `run_out_equals` in the compiled corpora), the suite's own mechanisms, which PLAN wrote down on 2026-09-17 without his yes ("Golden output where a value matters … Applied per test", `PLAN.md`; `archaeology.md` § 6). The reserved stop "an interpreter output a rung cannot account for" goes with it; the stop that remains is a test whose verdict changed other than the rung's own, which the gate sees.

Why: it grew from two one-off counts he agreed to into a standing three-run rule nobody put to him (archaeology § 5). In the rung reports the Opus review read it found no defect the suite missed; batch 4's eleven changed outputs all went from exit 0 to exit 1 and the gate would have caught them. Its cost was 27.2M of cache writes after waits over the batches, about half of 6.5b's new tokens, two to four hours of JVM time per batch, the box at load 8 to 36, one rung killing another's runner (row 532). The 18 tests that vary from run to run are all the team's own and pass or fail correctly (measures-6.5b.md). His words at 18:52 UTC: "If, if you need this like we if it's some like if it's necessary what you are saying, then we need to redesign how the test suite for Fortress is working. … why would you have to run it multiple times at the beginning to establish some kind of baseline? Like, what is the purpose of a test suit that you just cannot run it and get a green? If everything that's encoded in it is, is okay and it turns red if it's not, why would you have to compare some values that it outputs? Those values must be part of the test."

The one-time measurements his decisions name are kept, without a standing rule:

- Row 379 (2026-09-24), the count of interpreter tests whose output changes under walk's overflow check: taken, batch 4's rung O, landed. Nothing further.
- Row 330 (2026-09-29, R1), `floor` and `ceiling` on the float types, a library rung after the switch-over "with the count of interpreter tests whose output changes measured first": kept as one count for that rung.
- The numeral switch (2026-09-27, a numeral's type; 2026-09-29, option 3): Q-walk lands "with the changed interpreter outputs measured first": kept as one count for that rung.
- Rung Q's `IntLiteral` warning (2026-09-29, R8): "the rung measures where arithmetic lands under walk on the two microGPT programs and the interpreter tests before it lands: one measurement inside the rung": kept as that one measurement, in Q-lib.

How a named one-time count is taken: the batch record asks for it by name, quoting the decision that asks (protocol principle 5, the one new thing it is for). One edit pass over `ProjectFortress/tests/` compared against one base pass, masked as batch 5's Q2 masks (Java line numbers, identity hashes, moved library positions), the 18 unstable tests listed in one file under `coordinator/tools/` rather than found by a second base run. The base pass runs once for the batch, started in the background on the batch's base before the launch, never inside a rung and never twice; the edit pass is started by the worker in the background after its edit and read at the end of its steps, polled at 270 s. The runner and the comparison (`count-run.sh` and `compare-normalised.py`, rung F's, copied rung to rung since) move under `coordinator/tools/` when the first such rung is briefed, not tonight; none of the three rungs above is in batch 7b.

What catches an interpreter output that changes while its test still passes: the test, where the value matters; the skeptic's own differential programs on the constructs the rung touches (required as now); the gate's verdicts; the post-batch review's conformance reading. Nothing else, by design: his position is that the values that matter are part of the test and the suite's verdict is the check, so no standing net is offered, beside the suite or inside it (POSITIONS, "The suite's verdict is the check.").

Against his decisions: reverses none. 2026-09-24 (row 379) was taken once and is done; 2026-09-26 (rung C's and rung D's stops) narrowed what the stop meant and are kept as narrowings of the verdict stop; 2026-09-27 (reversible stops do not block) still governs the stops that remain; 2026-09-29 (R1, R8, the numeral switch) name one-time counts, kept above. His approval of batch 7's record (2026-09-27, "This is approved") was of its rungs and questions, and his go of 21:09 has 7b's record rewritten to the practice.

### (b) The review loops inside a batch

Default: the skeptic per rung stays, with its one refusal, judge, repair and second skeptic; the merged-diff review stays, once, beside the gate; its judge and repair run only for a finding that touches code, and the gate runs again after such a repair; a finding settled by tests and records goes to the next batch and is listed for him, without a judge; the second in-batch review is removed; the gate judge only for a red the repair did not answer (built 2026-09-29); the combined post-batch review stays and takes the count-table check.

Why: the review loop is 14.7% of all new tokens (25.8M) and 37% of batch N's; in the last four batches it stopped on owed tests, on the same red line the gate showed, and once on a defect of the Fortress change (7C's misstated sentence, row 490). Its judge-repair-second-review chain has twice held a green batch on tests-and-records findings (N, 6.5b), which his rule of 2026-09-29 already lets land. The second review sat alone on the critical path in N (17 minutes, 0.35M) and adds 3.0% over the batches. The skeptic is the best value per token on file: 10 of 14 misses in 6.5b, 11.4% of the spend.

Against his decisions: reverses none. 2026-09-24 ("Yes to both": the review's judge rules while the gate runs on) keeps the review beside the gate and its judge for a code finding; 2026-09-26 (a second ruling on the same rung or tree is Fable's) still applies where a second ruling happens (a red gate's judge after a review judge); 2026-09-28 (the combined review after every batch) is kept and grows by one check; 2026-09-29 (a review still blocking after its repair does not hold a green batch; the same weighing applies to the other rules) is what makes the routing the default.

What waits for him: the Opus review's option 1, removing the merged-diff review altogether and moving all its checks to the post-batch review, would reverse the "Yes to both" of 2026-09-24. It is not taken. It is listed for him in section 6 as the further step, with its saving (about 6.7% of the batches' new tokens, the review itself) and its cost (a conformance defect of the merged tree is pushed and repaired one batch later). Meanwhile the review runs once, beside the gate, as above.

### (c) Test names and assertion messages

Default, for every test written from tonight: named by topic, as the team's tests are, with no rung letter and no batch name; the path suffixes `Walk`, `Compiled`, `Checker`, `Link` stay where they say what a test exercises; no pointer line to a report; at most one comment line, saying what the program checks, which may name the ledger row it reproduces ("Those are like our bug reports", 20:53 UTC) and nothing else from the process record; an assertion message says what is checked and the expected answer in plain words; a specification rule is named by chapter or section, never by a `.tex` line; no ledger row, POSITIONS entry, FACTS title or PLAN item in a message; the ledger row and the report go in the commit message. The three homes are unchanged.

 ### How we work
 
 - **Test first, the test kept.** Every sealed-tree edit starts from a failing test added to the corpus: the worker writes the test first, verifies that it actually fails, makes the fix, proves it passes, and the test stays in the corpus from then on; the full suite stays green. The unacceptable process is the one-off validation script, proving once by hand that the interpreter and the compiler agree and leaving no permanent check. The batches fix the issues the explorations captured as ledger rows, each with how to reproduce it, "Those are like our bug reports": the worker first commits the reproduction into the test suite, "this is how I have reproduced what the previous probe has discovered", then makes the fix, and the test passing demonstrates that the issue is fixed; "There isn't much more to it." The test captures the essence of the problem, not the shape the probe met it in, "do not blindly transpose the issue from the probe like think about it what's the core problem and capture that", written as a clean minimal version. Whether the test was seen failing first is read from the worker's transcript, not shown by a committed capture. Whether the suite runs per edit or per landed batch is an engineering choice, and per batch is in line with the rule. Every measured and repaired defect gets a gated assertion, a deferred spec-settled one an `XXX` test.
+- **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test passes or fails, as the team designed the suite, and a value that matters is asserted in the test with the mechanisms the suite already has (an `assert` in an interpreter test, `run_out_equals` in a compiled one): "what is the purpose of a test suit that you just cannot run it and get a green? If everything that's encoded in it is, is okay and it turns red if it's not, why would you have to compare some values that it outputs? Those values must be part of the test." What a test prints beyond its checks does not matter: "When the designers of the test suite decided that it passes without any additional check, it is not needed to control its outputs." So no batch compares the corpus's printed outputs, no baseline is run to compare against, and no expected-output files are added to the interpreter suite, which has none; none of it is offered to him again.
 - **A deeper pass, not a halt.** When something goes wrong or turns out undecided, the answer is a deeper pass, not a halt or a rollback. On a red gate over a merged batch, no bisection of commits: "we should identify the source of the conflict holistically and rework that part in the merged batch", because the goal is one tree with everything running rather than the largest subset that happens to be green. On a divergence the specification does not settle, no stop: "it is not a reason to stop the climb, it is the reason to think harder, review the architecture and holistically decide on the best path forward and execute that one." What reaches him are the forks already reserved in `PLAN.md`, not new ones invented at the point of difficulty.
 - **Forks are probed before a batch is briefed.** "if there are known decision forks, which we can evaluate using probes, we should be doing these during this phase, during this planning phase": a fork a probe can settle is probed first, so that the decision is his and the worker gets a clean task, never a decision left to a worker and reviewed after the fact. Rows are taken one per message with refreshers (other languages, what makes sense in a high-performance language), not in groups.
 - **A brief describes the problem, not the solution.** "How do we prevent the myopic view? … I want to have full creativity of solutions": a worker that has not read our notes lists every way the language and the library offer before a design choice reaches him; a rule that blocks an option is answered with how the library gets around it (protocol principle 2). A worker that records timings records the CPU too, so that comparisons can be guessed at.
@@ -105,7 +106,7 @@
 - **The Fable rule.** "whenever it touches those three aspects of uh, library specification and implementation we are running the fable so if you use it sparingly I can pre-approve every such decision." The coordinator runs a Fable judgement without asking, sparingly, for a design question that touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation, once an Opus worker's evidence or list of ways is on file and the record has been searched and does not already settle it; he learns of it when the judgement is put to him in the ask form. He is asked first for any other Fable worker: a question about the coordinator's own conduct or a new kind of process choice, one whose recommendation would reverse a decision of his, or one where he wants Fable and Opus working independently. The standing pre-approvals: a judge's second ruling, and the top-tier reviews of the batch records.
 - **One review after every batch.** "run the conformance review after every batch", combined with the process review into one pass, since "the amortized cost here is well worth the benefit": one Opus reviewer, reading only, does the conformance review, the process measures against `reviews/process-review-6b-7-7R.md` (misses by kind, those of items in the rung's own briefing, map use, briefing cost, re-measuring) and the routing check; the coordinator files what it finds in `PLAN.md` at the landing.
 - **The phase-3 batches run on a standing go.** "I think you just carry on running the sequence of batches, I'll do the reset when I do it, If it stalls for a bit, I hope we'll recover without interruption. No need to complicate our runs with synchronization." And: "these are pre-approved. I want you to do autonomous overnight run." Each batch launches when the one before it has landed and its record is ready with no question open for him; a question a record raises goes to him first, except overnight, when it takes its recommended default and is listed for his review unless the default would reverse a decision of his, in which case that batch waits and the repair batch takes the slot; a run stalled by the limits is resumed with `resumeFromRunId`. A top-tier review in place of each coming batch record, in the form of `coordinator/climb-batch-7-review.md`, needs no further ask. The order is `PLAN.md`'s: batch 8 next. "Go" starts background work only; a batch run needs his explicit go, which for phase 3 this standing go is.
-- **The new batch practice, and what he expects of it.** The practice after the post-mortem of the batch practice: the synthesis of its two reviews and both archaeologies, written into the script, its manual and the protocol, the script reviewed, a batch record rewritten to it and run on it, the landed batches' committed scratch cleaned in parallel, all built; the post-mortem's four remaining questions (the output comparison, the review loops inside a batch, test names and messages, the cleaning's scope) take the synthesis's recommendations as defaults, listed for his review, unless a default would reverse a decision of his, in which case that part waits. "You can now redeem yourself by fixing this and, and, and showing me that you can be token efficient and not do bullshit jobs that you invented yourself." Every step spends the fewest workers the step needs and measures nothing the record already holds.
+- **The new batch practice, and what he expects of it.** The practice after the post-mortem of the batch practice: the synthesis of its two reviews and both archaeologies, written into the script, its manual and the protocol, the script reviewed, a batch record rewritten to it and run on it, the landed batches' committed scratch cleaned in parallel, all built; of the post-mortem's four remaining questions, the output comparison is settled by his own position ("The suite's verdict is the check."), the merged-diff review stays by his word ("A blocking second review does not hold a green batch."), new tests are named by topic, as he asked of the files named after batches, and the cleaning ran by kind on his rule that only the reports and the changes to the repository stay; the rest of the review loops inside a batch (no second review, a judge and a repair only for a finding in code) are the synthesis's defaults, in force. "You can now redeem yourself by fixing this and, and, and showing me that you can be token efficient and not do bullshit jobs that you invented yourself." Every step spends the fewest workers the step needs and measures nothing the record already holds.
 - **The gate's comparisons.** A comparison masks Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions, with every masked difference listed for him; the `testSystem` comparison is the sum of the four shards; a name comparison, red when a test that passed before is missing or failing, is a script change put to him on its own (parked, `PLAN.md`); row 366 waits; no route C entry goes into Proposed Features. A team test line the flat tower breaks is respelled keeping the value the test checks, no assertion deleted, every such line listed for him with its before and after.
 - **Estimates in the project's units.** Estimates in days or weeks are not accepted; sizes are given in the units the project has measured (a rung, a worker session, a check run). "I'm on a max plan. Talk to me in tokens." Costs are given in tokens, never in dollars, and a token count counts writes only, cache writes and new input: "Token counts, always report only writes. Cached reads are de-facto free vis-a-vis writes."
 - **Check-ins and stops.** A series of check-ins is spaced 45 minutes apart, since hourly ones risk "that this session KV cache is evicted and then the wake-up call pays the full" price; the one after a predicted process stop is a single extra. He sends messages at any time (a message during a turn is queued and kills nothing); he does not press stop while the session is working, including the seconds after a reply while the transcript backup runs; an accidental stop is said so, and the run is resumed, keeping every agent that had finished.
